summary:
Sejong stands under the national framework of South Korea, where gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

The sources record no Sejong-specific ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding touching trans people. What a visitor to Sejong faces is therefore the national legal position as the courts have shaped it, which is documented and enforceable rather than nominal.

Legal gender recognition no longer requires surgery anywhere in South Korea. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants who had not had sex-reassignment surgery, holding that conditioning a gender change on surgery is contrary to law and that judicial guidelines requiring surgery are now reference material rather than criteria. The court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity. The ruling removed the surgical prerequisite for a registered-sex change nationwide, including for residents of Sejong applying to their own court.

Restroom access is protected as a personal right and the state has been held liable for obstructing it. On 22 July 2024 the Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a claim of 3 million won, in a case brought by a person who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change from male to female in 2020 and was then advised by police to avoid women's public restrooms. The appellate court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right and that the police advice infringed personal rights.

Fear of using public facilities is widespread among trans people and is measured by a state body. A 2021 survey by the National Human Rights Commission of Korea of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% reported avoiding facilities out of fear.
tangentialFactors:
The protection documented here is judicial rather than legislative. The surgical prerequisite for legal gender recognition was removed by a regional court and the restroom claim succeeded in the appellate courts, while South Korean national law still contains no comprehensive anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation or gender identity, and no statute addressing restroom access, conversion practices or hate-motivated violence against trans people. A visitor cannot rely on a general equal-treatment code to do the work these judgments do case by case.

Hostility concentrates where the state's own procedures are involved or where crowds gather. The police advice in the restroom case came from a state officer, and the parent framework records a National Human Rights Commission of Korea finding in November 2023 that transgender patients face a blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare declined to draft hospitalisation guidelines. Anti-LGBT violence at public events and outing through contact tracing are documented at national level, so events, clinics and official interviews carry more turbulence than ordinary movement around Sejong does.

The military remains the sharpest documented zone of harm. Exclusion from service, the 2017 targeting of personnel under article 92-6, and Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su's compulsory discharge in 2020 and subsequent posthumous reinstatement set the outer boundary of what the national framework imposes; none of it applies to a civilian visitor, but it shapes the official climate a trans visitor enters.
localsOnly:
Residents changing their registered sex do so without a surgical requirement. The Yeongdong ruling of 8 May 2024 treated prior court guidelines mandating sex-reassignment surgery as reference rather than criteria, so applicants in Sejong can put their case to the court on hormone therapy and lived gender identity alone, and can argue physical integrity against a surgery condition.

The family-register route is the operative mechanism, and a completed change carries enforceable consequences. The plaintiff in the restroom case had received family-register gender change approval in 2020, which is what made the police advice to avoid women's restrooms actionable; the claim succeeded and the state paid 300,000 won, with comfortable restroom use affirmed as a fundamental and universal human right.

Residents harmed by facility avoidance or by official advice can document the pattern through the National Human Rights Commission of Korea, whose 2021 survey of 591 transgender respondents recorded 41% avoiding facilities out of fear. The Commission's own findings and its complaint route are part of the domestic machinery, alongside litigation for damages.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any Sejong court, Sejong municipal ordinance or Sejong agency has applied the Yeongdong reasoning or the restroom judgment is not sourced here; the inventory contains no Sejong-level decision, so the city-level position is unresolved rather than confirmed absent.

The size of the 300,000 won award relative to the 3 million won claim, and whether courts elsewhere award higher sums in comparable personal-rights cases, are not addressed by the sources.

Whether the removal of the surgical prerequisite has changed practice at family-registration offices in Sejong, as opposed to what courts will approve, is not sourced; no implementation data is given.

Enforcement of the finalised restroom judgment, including whether the state paid and whether police guidance was revised after 22 July 2024, is not documented in the inventory.
